How is Vermont organized, and who handles a house sale?

Vermont has 14 counties, but the day-to-day work of a house sale happens at the town level. The state's counties hold 237 towns and 10 cities, and each county has a seat that Vermonters call a shire town. Burlington is the shire town of Chittenden County, and our Burlington page covers that market in more detail.

That structure changes who you phone. The town clerk keeps the land records. The town listers set the appraised value that your property tax bill is built on. The Superior Court, which sits in each county, handles foreclosure and probate. If you are unsure which office owns a question, start with the clerk in the town where the house sits.

Where are Vermont deeds recorded?

Deeds are recorded at the town clerk's office in the town where the land lies, not at a county registry. Under 27 V.S.A. § 341, a deed must be signed by the seller, acknowledged before a notary public, and recorded in full in that clerk's office.

Two practical points follow for sellers:

  • If your deed refers to a survey made or revised after July 1, 1988, the survey has to accompany the deed or the deed has to cite where it is recorded.
  • If a sale splits a parcel or changes its boundaries, the deed needs a survey plat or a citation to the recorded boundaries.

The statute says a missed survey step does not void the deed. It can still slow a closing, so ask the clerk early.

What tax applies when a Vermont house is transferred?

Vermont charges a property transfer tax on the deed, and the buyer is liable for it unless the two sides agree otherwise. The base rate in 32 V.S.A. § 9602 is 1.25 percent of the value, or $1.00, whichever is greater. Different rates apply to some buyers.

SituationRate under 32 V.S.A. § 9602
General transfer1.25 percent of value
Buyer will use the home as a principal residence0.5 percent of the first $200,000, then 1.25 percent above that
Year-round residential property that will not be the buyer's principal residence and needs no landlord certificate3.4 percent of value

The 3.4 percent line was added by a 2025 act with an effective date of June 18, 2026. Because the buyer's intended use sets the rate, an investor purchase and an owner-occupant purchase of the same house can carry different tax bills.

Section 9603 lists transfers that are exempt. Two matter to many sellers:

  • Transfers between spouses, between parent and child, or between grandparent and grandchild, when no actual consideration is paid.
  • Transfers between the borrower and the lender in a foreclosure or a deed in lieu of foreclosure.

Property taxes are a separate matter and run through the town. Our Vermont property tax guide explains homestead declarations and appeals. As one example from the statute, an owner who disagrees with the listers' final decision has 14 days from the date of notice to appeal in writing to the board of civil authority by filing with the town clerk. That section is scheduled to be repealed on January 1, 2031, so confirm the current process with your town.

How does foreclosure work in Vermont, and how long does it take?

Vermont foreclosures run through the court. Chapter 172 of Title 12 requires the lender to file in the Civil Division of the Superior Court for the county where the land lies, and the case is heard by a judge without a jury. The lender also files a copy of the complaint with the town clerk.

The state allows more than one route:

  • Strict foreclosure. The court can end the owner's rights without a sale only if it finds no substantial value in the property above the debt and unpaid taxes. The redemption period is six months from the decree unless the court or the parties set a shorter one.
  • Judicial sale. The court orders a public sale if the owner does not redeem. For an owner-occupied dwelling house, no sale may take place within seven months of service of the complaint unless the court shortens the period or both sides agree.
  • Nonjudicial sale. Section 4961 excludes farmland and a dwelling house owned by a natural person, so this route is aimed at other property.

Owners can still redeem before a judicial sale by paying what the judgment requires. A foreclosed owner may also face a deficiency judgment if the lender asks for one before the confirmation order. The real timeline depends on where your own case stands, so talk to a Vermont attorney about your file.

If tenants live in the home, they must be named in the case, and a writ of possession cannot put the plaintiff in possession sooner than 30 days after it is served on them, or longer if federal law requires.

What happens when you inherit a house in Vermont?

Estates are handled by the Probate Division of the Superior Court, which also oversees wills and trusts. The Vermont Judiciary lists 14 probate division judges, and all estates fall under Title 14 of the Vermont Statutes Annotated.

The court describes two broad tracks:

  • Small estate. Available when the estate is worth under $45,000 and holds no real estate other than a timeshare.
  • Formal probate. Used when the person owned real estate or the estate is worth more than $45,000.

A house therefore puts most Vermont estates on the formal track. The court's forms include a motion for license to sell or convey real estate, so ask the probate court whether your estate needs one before you sign a contract. Heirs who want to understand taxes can read our Vermont estate and inheritance tax guide, and family transfers without payment may fall under the exemptions described above.

An out-of-state executor can serve, but the court asks for a Vermont resident or resident agent to accept legal papers for the estate.

What if tenants live in the house you want to sell?

A sale does not automatically end a tenancy, and a landlord needs a proper written notice. The notice periods in 9 V.S.A. § 4467 depend on the reason for ending the tenancy and on whether there is a written lease:

  • Nonpayment of rent: at least 14 days after actual notice.
  • Breach of a material term: at least 30 days before the termination date.
  • No written lease and monthly rent: 60 days for a tenant of two years or less, 90 days for longer.
  • No written lease and a landlord who has contracted to sell: at least 30 days.

With a written lease, a no-cause ending needs notice at least 30 days before the end of the term for tenancies of two years or less, and 60 days for longer ones. The notice has to state the termination date, and a court case must start within 60 days of that date. The provision on a sale speaks only to tenancies without a written lease, so a seller with a signed lease should ask a Vermont attorney how it is treated before promising a buyer an empty house. Our Vermont landlord and tenant guide goes through the steps, and our squatters and adverse possession page covers occupants who have no lease at all.

Do radon and other house conditions affect a Vermont sale?

Radon is the condition the state health department highlights most. The Vermont Department of Health says one in seven Vermont homes has elevated radon, and that testing is the only way to know. A buyer's inspector may ask about it, so a test result in hand can save time.

If your property has water, septic or foundation questions, ask the town clerk and a local inspector what a buyer is likely to raise.

What does a cash sale as-is mean in Vermont?

A cash sale as-is means the buyer takes the house in its current condition and does not need a mortgage to close. You skip listing prep, showings and most repair negotiation. You still deal with the same legal pieces as any seller: the deed is recorded at the town clerk, the buyer owes the transfer tax unless the contract says otherwise, and any mortgage or tax lien has to be paid at closing.

A cash sale can fit when the house is inherited, behind on payments, or occupied by tenants, because those situations often make a traditional listing slow. We buy houses across Vermont as-is. Call or text and we will talk through your situation and whether a cash sale suits it.

Frequently asked questions

How many counties does Vermont have?

Vermont has 14 counties, which together contain 237 towns and 10 cities. Much of the paperwork for a sale happens at the town clerk's office instead of a county office.

Where do I record a deed in Vermont?

At the clerk's office of the town where the land lies. The deed must be signed and acknowledged before a notary.

Who pays the Vermont property transfer tax?

The buyer is liable unless the parties agree otherwise. The general rate is 1.25 percent of value, with lower and higher rates in some cases.

Is Vermont foreclosure judicial?

Mostly yes. Lenders file in Superior Court in the county where the land lies. Nonjudicial sale is not available for farmland or a dwelling house owned by an individual.

How long does a Vermont owner have to redeem after a decree?

Six months from the decree unless the court orders a shorter period or the parties agree to one.

Do I need probate to sell an inherited house?

A house usually puts the estate on the formal track. Ask the Probate Division whether a license to sell real estate is needed.

Can I sell a house with tenants?

Yes, but a sale does not end a lease. Notice rules are in 9 V.S.A. § 4467.
